COMMENTS OF INVENERGY RENEWABLES LLC AND INVENERGY THERMAL 
LLC 
 
Invenergy Renewables LLC and Invenergy Thermal LLC (collectively, “Invenergy”) 
respectfully submit these comments in response to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s 
(“FERC” or “Commission”) February 20, 2025, Order to Show Cause1 and PJM Interconnection, 
L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) March 24, 2025, answer in the above-captioned proceeding.2 
As the Commission has acknowledged, data centers, advanced manufacturing, and 
electrification are spurring significant load growth. By 2028, data centers alone will account for 
up to 12% of national electricity consumption, exceeding even relatively recent load forecasts.3 
As a result, the Commission and regional transmission organizations are reexamining existing 
policies to ensure they can satisfy these new demands. PJM, the Midcontinent Independent

System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”), and the Southwest Power Pool, Inc. (“SPP”), for instance, have 
all proposed upending long-standing interconnection procedures for short-term, and Invenergy 
would argue sometimes illusory, benefits.4 But regardless of the merits of those individual 
proposals, they share a common feature: they are reactive, rather than proactive. They do not 
improve load forecasting, facilitate needed transmission deployment, or establish generally-
applicable market rules that facilitate long-term investment to accommodate new, large loads.  
This Show Cause proceeding is a needed first step to address these broader issues, but as 
Invenergy sets forth below, the Commission should not stop upon adopting rules for co-located 
large loads. Rather, it should seize this opportunity to articulate a new, proactive paradigm for 
jointly studying large-load interconnection requests as part of the generator interconnection 
queue, thereby ensuring that RTOs/ISOs engage in coordinated load, interconnection, and 
transmission planning that enhances resource adequacy and reliability, while efficiently 
deploying generation and allocating scarce transmission where it is most needed.  
The Commission should also consider other, economical alternatives for addressing load 
growth. Therefore, in addition to adopting an integrated planning process, the Commission 
should ensure that RTOs/ISOs properly value and compensate merchant transmission for its 
reliability and economic benefits.5 While Invenergy acknowledges this issue is outside the scope 
of this proceeding, it encourages the Commission to adopt policies that better facilitate merchant 
transmission as part of its holistic consideration of how to address large load growth.  
With regard to this Show Cause proceeding, Invenergy offers the following high-level

principles that should guide co-location policy.  
I.   COMMENTS 
 
A. Large Loads Should be Studied in a Combined Queue with Generation and 
Transmission Interconnection. 
 
PJM, in its response to the Show Cause Order,6 proposes to continue its bifurcated 
approach to studying co-located loads and generation, wherein network load interconnection 
requests are studied under Attachment M-3 and co-located generator modifications are studied in 
the generator interconnection and necessary study process,7 while non-network loads will only 
employ the necessary study used for generator interconnections. Invenergy respectfully 
encourages the Commission and PJM to dispense with this bifurcated process and to instead 
jointly study large load and generator interconnection requests. Doing so would more efficiently 
use the transmission system and decrease ratepayer costs.  
Under PJM’s existing rules, PJM’s standardized interconnection procedures only apply to 
generation and transmission interconnection, but PJM uses the Attachment M-3 process for load 
interconnections. Attachment M-3 establishes a local planning process in which PJM and 
transmission owners process load interconnection requests and plan local upgrades and 
supplemental projects in response to identified load needs.8  While Attachment M-3 has been 
used to incorporate large load additions into the PJM system, it was originally intended as a 
transmission planning process for supplemental projects, not as a process to interconnect large 
loads. As a result, it has several characteristics that make it unsuitable for large load 
 
6 Show Cause Order at P 88, subsection d. 
7 PJM Answer at 8, 48-49. 
8 PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff (“PJM Tariff”), Attachment M-3.  See also PJM Answer at 6-7 (explaining 
the “traditional load interconnection processes” includes the “Transmission Owner retail load integration study” to 
identify local upgrades based on local transmission owner planning criteria and PJM’s “Do No Harm study” to 
evaluate supplemental project’s impact on the transmission system).

DCACTIVE-79938279.1 
 
 
 
 
 
 
4 
 
 
interconnection.  
First, Attachment M-3 does not consider transmission solutions outside of a particular 
transmission owner’s footprint, artificially excluding potentially less-expensive solutions. 
Second, because load additions are primarily studied under local transmission owner study 
processes using a different set of study assumptions, models and timelines, than generator 
interconnection studies, the load and generator study processes may each identify network 
upgrades that would not be necessary were these processes combined, resulting in overbuilding 
of the PJM system at significant expense. Third, because of the independent study processes, 
large load additions may not get factored into generator interconnection studies in a timely 
manner, or could be factored in but then never materialize. This creates significant opacity and 
risk for generators, thereby stifling development that might occur were generation developers 
provided more clarity on planned load interconnections.   
Finally, there is little, if any, transparency on how M-3 studies are conducted, or the 
timeline for completing such studies.  Large load interconnection customers are already facing 
interconnection delays as a result of this uncertainty, and the lack of transparency is creating 
opportunities for undue discrimination that will decrease competition and raise systemwide costs.  
These defects, however, can be remedied by adopting a joint study process that requires 
large loads – those over 50 MW or interconnecting to facilities at voltages greater than 115kV –
be studied along with generation and transmission interconnection requests. Combining load 
interconnection with generation and transmission into a standardized study process would 
promote transparency and ensure that network upgrades identified and allocated to 
interconnection customers correctly reflect the expected topology of the system.  It would also 
address a number of concerns raised in the Show Cause Order because transmission use, co-

DCACTIVE-79938279.1 
 
 
 
 
 
 
5 
 
 
location impacts on the transmission system, and cost allocation would be addressed in a single 
study process.9  
Moreover, if load and generation have not already identified one another, a common 
interconnection queue can match appropriate generation to the load, mitigating the uncertainty 
that can result from uncertain load forecasting. While PJM notes that large load aggregations 
could be included in regional transmission planning as part of the yearly load-forecasting 
process,10 it is unclear how often this occurs or what aggregation would trigger planning for large 
load additions in regional planning.  Load forecasts also are just that, a forecast, and may never 
materialize. Folding large load requests into the interconnection queue will reduce guesswork 
and reduce speculative load interconnection requests. 
Invenergy recognizes that incorporating large load interconnections into the generation 
queue across the PJM footprint will involve stakeholder and state engagement.  In crafting these 
rules, Invenergy makes the following suggestions: 
• Large load interconnection requests should be part of the standard interconnection 
queue with assigned queue positions. This will increase transparency for load and 
developers, while also ensuring equitable treatment of load and generation as they 
interconnect to the transmission system.  
• PJM could establish commercial readiness criteria or security deposits for large 
load interconnection requests akin to those required for generator interconnection 
requests, thereby reducing speculative large load interconnection requests and 
incentivizing large loads to materialize.  
• Like generator interconnection requests, large load interconnection requests could 
withdraw from the queue if they are no longer viable, with appropriate penalties 
to offset the harm to other interconnection customers. 
Given that PJM is currently completing its interconnection queue transition process, these

new rules could reasonably commence with New Cycle # 1, which is projected to begin April 
2026.  In the interim, PJM’s Tariff should be amended to include at least co-located loads in the 
standard generator interconnection procedures. Studying co-located load and generators together 
will reduce the chance of overbuilding the system and ensure costs for network upgrades are 
assigned consistent with the Commission’s cost allocation policies. 
B. Co-Location Arrangements Must Include Safeguards to Ensure Other 
Interconnection Customers are Not Harmed. 
 
PJM in its Answer identifies numerous avenues for adding large co-located loads. One of 
those proposals, “New Option 6,” would permit large loads interconnecting as Network Load to 
bring its own generation to PJM. PJM explains that it might consider mechanisms to process 
these types of interconnection requests more quickly.11 While Invenergy welcomes 
improvements that expedite the interconnection process, any such changes must be adopted on a 
non-discriminatory, queue-wide basis, and not only for preferenced generators. Moreover, to the 
extent the Commission approves New Option 6, it should adopt reasonable safeguards to ensure 
that other interconnection customers are not harmed by co-location arrangements, for instance by 
maintaining queue priority on a first-ready, first-served basis; preventing co-located load from 
getting priority access to available transmission system headroom; and ensuring that PJM’s 
processing of co-location interconnection requests does not deprive PJM of the resources needed 
to process the interconnection queue. Such limitations would be in keeping with the 
Commission’s long-standing policy against queue jumping.12 
 
11 PJM Answer at 17 (explaining that PJM could accelerate interconnection studies of new generation, enhance 
provisional interconnection service options at discrete study points to accelerate generation’s ability to reach 
commercial operation, and that states could remove barriers to entry by assuming cost responsibility for 
transmission upgrades pursuant to the State Agreement Approach to encourage large load development in their 
jurisdictions). 
12 See, e.g., Standardization of Generator Interconnection Agreements and Procedures, Order No. 2003, 104 FERC 
¶ 61,103, at P 35 (2003), reh’g, Order No. 2003-A, 106 FERC ¶ 61,220, reh’g, Order No. 2003-B, 109 FERC ¶

7 
 
 
C. PJM Should Include a Transition Process Until its New Co-Location Rules are 
Effective. 
 
While this Show Cause proceeding could result in new rules accommodating additional 
co-location configurations and should include a combined interconnection process for load and 
generation, properly issuing new rules takes time and benefits from a robust stakeholder process.   
Therefore, while new comprehensive rules are developed, PJM should implement a 
transition process so that large loads customers can move forward with co-location arrangements 
in the short-term if they so choose. To reduce study timelines and avoid significant modifications 
to the PJM system while new rules are being fashioned, large-load customers should be allowed 
to pursue behind-the-meter configurations with new generating facilities in development and 
without being considered network load, and protections should be required to prevent that load 
from accessing the grid.  To the extent such protections are not available, behind-the-meter load 
should be charged commensurate with its expected transmission system use, but less than fully 
network load.

DCACTIVE-79938279.1 
 
 
 
 
 
 
8 
 
 
II. CONCLUSION 
 
Invenergy respectfully requests that PJM and the Commission consider these comments 
in determining how PJM’s tariff could be amended to include just and reasonable rules for co-
located load and generation. 
 
 
Respectfully submitted,
